ca_table_scraps_pinnacle.blurb: A compact bolted pinnacle on Mount St. Helena above Calistoga, in the wine country north of the Bay Area. Roughly 13 single-pitch sport lines run about 60 feet, so it suits a short session. Grades start with an easy 5.4, bunch up from 5.7 through 5.10, and top out with a couple of 5.11s, which makes it friendly to newer leaders as well as people working toward harder numbers. The climbing is on cobbles, pinches and jugs, and the routes have lower-off anchors. It sits in dry chaparral and oak country, and the stone can bake in the sun, so choose your day with temperature in mind.

ca_ruby_peak.blurb: A high alpine peak above Ruby Lake in the Little Lakes Valley and Mono Recesses of the Eastern Sierra, with east-facing walls that catch morning light and sit in shade later in the day. Most of the 13 climbs are alpine routes, with one trad line. They range from fourth-class terrain and easy 5th class up through plenty of 5.10 and a couple of 5.11 pitches. Expect a long walk-in that finishes cross-country, thin air at this elevation, quality that varies from solid to flaky, and weather that can turn fast. It is a committed day, best for parties comfortable on alpine granite and moving efficiently.
ca_ruby_peak.parking_note: Leave the car at the Mosquito Flat trailhead, at the top of the paved Rock Creek Road.
ca_ruby_peak.approach: From the Mosquito Flat trailhead, walk the Little Lakes Valley trail, then the Mono Pass trail, up to Ruby Lake. Leave the maintained trail there and continue cross-country over brush, wet ground and boulders to the base of the wall.

ca_plasma_wall.blurb: Plasma Wall is a sport wall on the limestone ridge known as the other Lover's Leap, in far northern California above Scott Valley. All 13 routes are bolted, and they are hard: about half are 5.11 and half 5.12, with a single 5.13. The left end is grey and slabby to vertical, while the right side swings into steep white and orange rock. It is rated as some of the best stone on the ridge, second only to the Room next door. The wall picks up morning sun and has big valley views. This is a destination for people already climbing 5.11 and up.

ca_rexrodes.blurb: A small, quieter crag on the south side of Mount Woodson in north San Diego County, known mostly for crack climbing. Of the 13 climbs, twelve are trad or top-rope lines and one is a boulder problem. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10 range, so it favors climbers who already lead moderate to hard cracks, though a few easier lines exist. The approach is short, and the crag draws fewer people than the main Woodson boulders. Watch for rattlesnakes on the walk in, particularly in warm weather.

ca_lost_world.blurb: A remote cluster of granite walls just off the Sonora Pass Highway, near Donnell Lake. About a dozen routes are spread across several faces, seven bolted and five trad, from one pitch to four. Grades start at a lone 5.8, with most of the climbing in the 5.10 and 5.11 range and a couple of 5.12s, so it suits confident leaders. The walls are scattered and mostly unclimbed beyond these lines, and the walk in is a long downhill hike on faint trail, so remember you must climb back up at the end. Many routes are 60 to 100 feet.

ca_mcleod_lake.blurb: A compact east-facing granite wall just beyond McLeod Lake, in the Lakes Basin above Mammoth Lakes at roughly 9,300 feet. Twelve single-pitch routes, mostly 50 to 70 feet, cluster around the 5.10 range, with a few easier lines and one 5.11. The rock is good but a little dirty in spots, so test holds. Being east-facing it gets early sun and stays cool through much of a summer day, and snow can linger at the base into late June. A calm alternative when Horseshoe Slabs is crowded. The walk includes some route-finding.
ca_mcleod_lake.parking_note: Park in the Horseshoe Lake lot at the end of Lake Mary Road, above Mammoth Lakes.
ca_mcleod_lake.approach: Take the trail toward McLeod Lake, then branch onto a faint side path near the catch-and-release sign. Follow the buried water pipe to a silver post with yellow bands, take the left fork and cross the small stream, then keep left below broken rock to the main cliff.
